learn.title: Asking where a variable lives
learn.body: Every variable sits somewhere in memory. In C you can ask for that location with the `&` operator. Writing `&n` means the address of `n`. It is not the value in `n`: it is where `n` is kept.

learn.title: Printing an address
learn.body: `%p` prints an address in hex and expects a `void *`, so we cast. The number you see is different on different machines and even between runs. Never rely on a specific address.

learn.title: Neighbours in memory
learn.body: Array items sit side by side. The address of `a[1]` is exactly one `int` after the address of `a[0]`, which is 4 bytes. For a `char` array it is just 1 byte. You can see this by subtracting the addresses.

learn.title: Measuring the gap
learn.body: This prints 4, then 1. `uintptr_t` from `stdint.h` is an integer type big enough to hold an address, so we can subtract.

learn.title: Reading it back
learn.body: Use the output 4 and 1 from the program above.
steps: Items of an `int` array are 4 bytes apart
Items of a `char` array are 1 byte apart
The gap equals the size of one item

learn.body: Do not print addresses in your tests and expect the same text. Use them to understand your program, not as stable values.

questions.prompt: The \_\_ operator gives the address of a variable.

questions.explanation: `&` asks where the variable is stored.

questions.prompt: Will `printf("%p\n", (void *)&n);` print the same address every run?
questions.explanation: The system may place variables in different spots, so never depend on an address.

questions.prompt: `int a[3]` is stored in a row. How many bytes apart are `&a[0]` and `&a[1]`?
questions.explanation: Each `int` is 4 bytes, so the next item starts 4 bytes later.

questions.prompt: `char c[3]` is stored in a row. How many bytes apart are `&c[0]` and `&c[1]`?
Match each piece to what it does.
pairs: integer big enough for an address
questions.explanation: These four pieces are the toolkit for looking at addresses.

questions.prompt: Which lets you subtract two addresses as plain integers?
questions.explanation: `uintptr_t` is made to hold an address as an integer.
